extracted.intended_audience: Variety readers / general entertainment and TV industry audience
extracted.subtask_description: A news story reporting on criticism and controversy involving a late-night television host, including political reactions, network decisions, and broadcast standards. Focuses on factual reporting, quoted statements, and context about ratings and network policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments for cancellation based on perceived lack of talent and ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Trump urged CBS to pull the plug on Colbert’s show 'NOW' instead of ending its run next May, calling him 'a pathetic trainwreck, with no talent or anything else necessary for show business success' and saying 'CBS should, ‘put him to sleep,’ NOW, it is the humanitarian thing to do!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim attacks used as justification: claims of no talent, running on 'hatred and fumes,' and 'nonexistent ratings' are presented as grounds for immediate cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for labeling the 'worst' late-night host (per Trump)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Who has the worst Late Night host, CBS, ABC, or NBC??? They all have three things in common: High Salaries, No Talent, REALLY LOW RATINGS!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets out three evaluative dimensions invoked by the critic: salary level, perceived talent, and ratings performance — used here as a negative ranking metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network cancellation criterion: financial/economic viability
rubrics_metrics.description: CBS, in announcing the cancellation of 'The Late Show,' insisted the move was 'purely a financial decision' that came after a years-long decline in the economics of late-night TV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece frames network decisions about show renewals/cancellations primarily around economic metrics (ratings decline, advertising/revenue trends) rather than solely content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast license revocation argument tied to editorial slant (per Trump)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If Network NEWSCASTS, and their Late Night Shows, are almost 100% Negative to President Donald J. Trump, MAGA, and the Republican Party, shouldn’t their very valuable Broadcast Licenses be terminated? I say, YES!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This articulates a policy/criteria claim that consistent negative coverage could justify termination of broadcast licenses — presented as the president's proposal, not as established law or practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBS News style guidance on institutional naming
rubrics_metrics.description: CBS News' standards department instructed staffers last week to continue to refer to the original Kennedy Center name in their coverage. 'If the president or other administration officials use the new name in a soundbite that is their prerogative,' the news org said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A newsroom standard: preserve the established name in coverage while allowing verbatim use of sources' own naming in soundbites; distinguishes reporting language from quoted language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program labeling and on-air crediting for specials
rubrics_metrics.description: In its Dec. 23 broadcast of the Kennedy Center Honors, a voiceover lead-in said, 'And now, the Trump Kennedy Center Honors on CBS,' and an on-screen graphic said, 'The following is a Donald J. Trump and Kennedy Center Production.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates obligations/practices around program lead-ins and on-screen credits for special broadcasts — how a program is presented and attributed to producers/hosts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-night host performance elements (satire, impersonation, fact-checking, jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of Colbert's approach: mocking Trump's hosting takeover, performing an impression ('I don’t know how much effort I’m putting into the impression [of Trump] anymore'), playing Trump's remarks, fact-checking (pointing out that Jimmy Kimmel never hosted the Honors while Colbert did), and satirical quips (e.g., FIFA 'Peace Prize' jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes substantive comedic techniques and content features that characterize a late-night monologue: satire, impersonation, use of actual clips/remarks, factual corrections for comedic effect, and absurdist comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reaction as a metric of monologue effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes audience boos when Colbert said 'This year’s Kennedy Center Honors ceremony is the very first since Trump installed himself as chair of the Kennedy Center’s board,' indicating the live audience's disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience response (boos, laughs) is presented as an immediate reception metric that signals how a monologue line landed in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast profanity standards / censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert told the president, 'Go fuck yourself' (with the f-word censored).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates broadcast standards in practice: profanity may be used for emphasis but is subject to censorship on network television; reporters note censorship when relevant to content.
